analysis.one_liner: Admits most of Washington, D.C. as a new state with two senators and one House member.
analysis.headline: The House Oversight Committee voted 21–16 to send the bill toward the floor, but the full House never voted on it before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would turn most of Washington, D.C. into a new state, called Washington, Douglass Commonwealth, while keeping a smaller federal zone — the White House, Capitol, Supreme Court, and main monuments — under direct federal control as the 'Capital.' D.C.'s roughly 700,000 residents would gain full voting representation in Congress: two senators and one voting House member. Today they elect only a non-voting delegate and have no vote in the Senate. The bill set up a transition in which the federal government keeps paying for some courts, prosecutors, and benefits until the new state takes over.
analysis.who_benefits: Washington, D.C. residents, who currently have no voting member of Congress and no senators. They would gain two senators and one voting House member, equal footing with other states, and full control over their own laws subject to the Constitution. Federal employees and retirees with D.C.-linked pensions would keep their benefits during the transition.

how_it_helps.text: Admits most of the District of Columbia into the Union as the State of Washington, Douglass Commonwealth on equal footing with the other states.
Gives the new state two senators and one voting representative, elected by D.C. residents, and permanently raises the House to 436 members.
Carves out a smaller federal 'Capital' containing the White House, Capitol, Supreme Court, federal office buildings, and principal monuments, preserving the constitutional seat of government.

Continues certain federal responsibilities during the transition — retirement benefits, courts, prosecutions, and college tuition assistance — until the new state certifies it is ready to take them over.

analysis.who_pays: No direct new tax; the state may not tax federal property, and the federal government keeps title to its lands and funds some courts, prosecutors, and benefits until the state takes over. The political cost falls on the existing Senate, which would gain two new members chosen by a heavily Democratic electorate, changing its balance of power.
analysis.who_pays_short: Existing Senate balance; federal taxpayers marginally

drawbacks.text: The bill creates two new Senate seats and one House seat, changing the Senate's political balance — the core objection raised by opponents.

Constitutional question: the 23rd Amendment still gives the federal district presidential electors, so the bill provides only an expedited process for a separate amendment to repeal it [S2][S4]. A constitutional amendment requires two-thirds of both chambers and approval by 38 states, far beyond this bill alone, so critics argue full statehood may ultimately require one.
The small population living in the remaining federal 'Capital' would vote in federal elections in their last state of domicile, an unusual arrangement that could be contested.
The federal government continues funding courts, prosecutors, marshals, and certain benefits until the state certifies readiness, a real transition cost to federal taxpayers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the roughly 700,000 Americans without voting representation in Congress, the gain — two senators and a voting representative — is large and immediate. The main counterweights are the constitutional uncertainty around admitting a state from the federal district by ordinary legislation, and the deliberate political consequence of two new Senate seats, which opponents see as the bill's true purpose. The bill tries to address the district problem by carving out the monuments and federal buildings and setting up repeal of the 23rd Amendment, but that repeal would face a much higher bar than this bill did.

outcome.mechanism: The bill cleared committee — reported on June 18, 2020, and placed on the House calendar of bills awaiting floor action — but House leadership never brought it up for a vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Del. Eleanor Holmes Norton introduced the bill on February 7, 2020; it was referred to five House committees, with Oversight and Government Reform taking the lead.
On February 11, 2020, the Oversight Committee held a markup and voted 21–16 to order the bill reported with amendments.

On June 18, 2020, the committee reported the bill, the four other committees were discharged from further consideration, and the bill was placed on the Union Calendar — the House's list of bills ready for possible floor action.
No Representative cosponsored the bill besides its sponsor, and the full House never voted on it before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The status quo held. D.C. residents remained without voting representation in Congress, and opponents of adding two new senators kept the Senate's composition unchanged. Supporters had at least moved the bill out of committee, but that produced no law.

sides.party_line_note: The only recorded vote was the Oversight Committee's 21–16 vote to report the bill, which the record does not break down by party [S6]; the bill drew zero cosponsors [S5], and D.C. statehood divides Congress almost entirely along party lines.

industries.note: The bill would add two senators and one House member, diluting every sitting member's share of power and shifting the Senate's balance. The people who vote on whether to enfranchise D.C. are the same people whose chamber composition would change — which is why the bill sat without a floor vote despite clearing committee.

industries.industry: Federal government (as landholder and service provider)
industries.note: Even as it creates a new state, the bill locks in federal control: the smaller 'Capital' stays under federal jurisdiction, federal property cannot be taxed by the state, military lands remain under exclusive federal authority, and the federal government keeps paying for courts, prosecutors, and benefits until the state certifies readiness.
